lead: A regular expression is a short pattern that names a set of strings. For example, ^baa+!$ names b, then two or more a, then !. A finite-state automaton is a machine with states and labeled arcs. It reads a string once, left to right, and says accept or reject. The two views are equivalent: every pattern has an automaton, and every such automaton has a pattern. NLP uses this for tokenization, spelling rules, and morphology.
prereq: You need: strings and sets, plus the idea of language layers from chapter 1.2.

blocks.text: A regular expression (regex) is a pattern over an alphabet Σ, a finite set of symbols. The language L(R) of pattern R is the set of strings that R matches. For example, with Σ = {a,b,!}, the pattern baa+! has language {baa!, baaa!, baaaa!, ...}.
L(R) = { w ∈ Σ* | w matches R }
blocks.where: L(R) is the language of pattern R; w is a string; Σ* is the set of all finite strings over alphabet Σ.

items: a literal matches itself; concatenation ab matches a then b.
Kleene star a* matches zero or more a. Plus a+ matches one or more; ? matches zero or one.
[a-z] matches one character in the range; [^0-9] matches one character not a digit; . matches any one character.
^ anchors to string start; $ anchors to string end. Without anchors a pattern may match a substring.
Parentheses group; backslash escapes a metacharacter, so \. is a literal dot.

blocks.text: Precedence: star, then concatenation, then union; use parentheses to be clear.

An NFA (nondeterministic finite automaton) has states, a start state, final states, and arcs labeled by symbols or by ε. ε is the empty string: an epsilon jump consumes no input. From one state an NFA may have several arcs with the same symbol, or an ε arc. It accepts a string if some path from start to a final state spells the string.

items: A literal symbol becomes two states joined by that symbol.
Concatenation joins fragments: final of one to start of next.
Union R|S adds a new start with ε arcs to both fragments, and ε arcs from both finals to a new final.
Star R* adds a new start and a new final with four ε arcs: new start → new final (skip), new start → R's start (enter), R's final → new final (exit), and R's final → R's start (repeat).

blocks.text: Each operator adds at most two states and some ε arcs. For baa+!, plus is one or more: write it as b a a a* !. The NFA has a loop for extra a. The DFA in the figure has q0 start, q4 final, and q3 looping on a.

A DFA (deterministic finite automaton) is an NFA with two restrictions: no ε arcs, and at most one arc per symbol from each state; if we insist on a total machine, missing arcs all go to one non-final dead state. It is easy to run: keep one current state, read one symbol, follow one arc. If no arc exists, the machine dies and rejects.

items: The DFA start state is the ε-closure of the NFA start: the set of NFA states reachable by ε alone.
For a DFA state S and symbol c, move to the ε-closure of all NFA states reachable from any state in S on c.
Repeat for every new set. A DFA state is final if it contains any NFA final state.

blocks.text: The number of DFA states is finite, at most 2k for k NFA states. For baa+! the equivalent DFA is the table:
q0 is start; q4 is final. A dash means no arc.

sections.h3: What a finite machine cannot count

blocks.text: A finite automaton has a fixed, finite number of states. That is its only memory. It cannot store an unbounded count. So no regular expression or finite automaton can match the language {a<sup>n</sup>b<sup>n</sup> | n ≥ 1}: n a's followed by n b's. To check equal counts for every n, the machine would need to remember how many a's it has seen, and n can grow without limit. The same limit blocks balanced parentheses, brackets and XML tags.
Real regex engines add backreferences and recursion, which go beyond this model. Standard regular expressions do not.

A finite-state transducer is the same machine with an output symbol on each arc. It maps one string to another, which is how morphological rules are compiled; see chapter 1.6. Tokenizers also use patterns; see chapter 1.4. Counting needs context-free grammars, covered in Unit 3.

spec.aria: Five states q0 to q4 in a row joined by b, a, a and exclamation mark, with a loop on a at q3 and q4 final; three trace bars below show baa and baaa accepted and ba rejected at q2.

examples.question: Write a regular expression for the sheep language: a word is b, then at least two a, then !. Draw a deterministic automaton. Check baa!, baaa! and ba!.
steps: Alphabet {a,b,!}. After b, at least two a means b, a, then one or more a, then !. So the pattern is b a a+ !.
Add anchors: ^baa+!$. ^ is start, $ is end, + means one or more of the previous a. The shortest match is baa!.
Build a DFA with 5 states q0 to q4: q0 start, q4 final. Arcs: q0-b->q1, q1-a->q2, q2-a->q3, q3-a->q3, q3-!->q4.
Check baa!: q0-b->q1-a->q2-a->q3-!->q4. q4 is final, so accepted = 1.
Check baaa!: q0-b->q1-a->q2-a->q3-a->q3-!->q4. q4 is final, so accepted = 1.
Check ba!: q0-b->q1-a->q2. Next is !, but q2 has no ! arc. The machine dies, so rejected = 0.
examples.answer: The pattern is ^baa+!$. The DFA has 5 states. baa! is accepted (1), baaa! is accepted (1), ba! is rejected (0).
examples.check:
import re
pat = r'^baa+!$'
print(5)
for s in ['baa!', 'baaa!', 'ba!']:
    print(1 if re.fullmatch(pat, s) else 0)

traps: Star * matches zero or more, so ab* matches a and ab; plus + is one or more.
A pattern without ^ and $ can match part of a string; ab matches abc.
Character classes match one character, not a word.
Standard regex cannot match a<sup>n</sup>b<sup>n</sup> or balanced brackets; backreferences are an extension, not finite-state.
Escaping matters: . is any character, \. is a literal dot.

quiz.a: Zero or more a, including the empty string.

quiz.q: Why add ^ and $ to a pattern?
quiz.a: To require a whole-string match; without them the engine can find a substring.

quiz.q: Write a regex for b, at least two a, then !, and trace baa! on its DFA.
quiz.a: ^baa+!$. Trace: q0 -b-> q1 -a-> q2 -a-> q3 -!-> q4. q4 is final, so accept.

quiz.q: Trace baaa! on the same DFA.
quiz.a: q0 -b-> q1 -a-> q2 -a-> q3 -a-> q3 -!-> q4. q4 final, so accept.

quiz.q: Why can no DFA match a<sup>n</sup>b<sup>n</sup> for all n?
quiz.a: It has finitely many states, so it cannot store an unbounded count n. Equal counts need unbounded memory.

quiz.q: In subset construction, what is a DFA state, and when is it final?
quiz.a: A set of NFA states. It is final if it contains any NFA final state.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industry regex engines such as PCRE and RE2 add optimizations; RE2 keeps linear-time finite-state matching. Log parsing, form validation and bioinformatics use patterns daily. Finite-state transducers power mobile keyboards and morphology engines. Search next for Thompson construction, subset construction, and finite-state transducer morphology.
